description:
The best upcoming passes over a location, ranked by the rating seeksat.com shows ("what's the best pass tonight?"): best is the top pass and passes the top limit (default 3, up to 20), each naming its satellite. Which pass tool: find_passes lists passes in time order, from the next one (limit 1) to every pass in the window; find_best_pass ranks them by rating, for one satellite or, with none named, from a scan of many ("what can I see tonight?"); get_radio_pass gives one pass's Doppler and tuning, the next one by default. For what is up at this moment use find_satellites_up_now; to draw the winning pass set chart:true, or give a pass's peak time to get_pass_chart.

What it searches. With satellite: that satellite's passes, the top limit and not every pass. Without, a scan: visual mode (default) covers the popular satellites plus CelesTrak's visual group of the brightest objects, over 72 hours (up to 168); radio mode covers every satellite with known downlinks over 24 hours (up to 72), optionally only those with a downlink in bands or of a kind in modes. A scan leaves out satellites whose elements are more than 14 days old and counts what it skipped.

mode "visual" (default) keeps only the part of each pass that can be seen by eye, so rise and set can fall mid-sky and the peak is the highest point of that part; mode "radio" keeps the whole pass above minElevation. Rise and set are where it crosses minElevation, not the horizon, so a higher minElevation gives shorter, fewer passes.

rating is the one seeksat.com shows. Visual mode: how much brighter than the faintest visible star for skyType the pass gets (headroomMag); the cloud forecast (up to 4 days ahead) never changes the rating: it is named in reason and in the cloud fields of each row, and ranking counts a cloudy forecast as Poor and some cloud as one level lower (good, ok, low); at most Fair when the brightness is estimated, the peak is below 15 degrees or it is seen for under a minute, at most Good below 25 degrees or when seen for under 2 minutes, and Excellent only above 40 degrees. Radio mode: the peak height, a bar lower for each 6 dB of extra path loss beyond 2,000 km, and at most Fair when SatNOGS stations tried at least 3 times in 30 days and heard nothing.

Ranking. Visual: rating bars, then a measured brightness before an estimated one, then headroomMag, then captureProbability, with the cloud forecast folded in where it reaches. Radio scans: satellites a hobby receiver can tune (30 MHz to 1 GHz) first unless bands is given, then rating bars, then how recently SatNOGS stations heard it (48 hours, 7 days, 30 days, unknown, probably silent), then how often, then peak elevation, then captureProbability. Unknown reception never holds a satellite down. Reception data is from SatNOGS Network (CC BY-SA 4.0).

An empty result comes with a note saying why. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change. A place name is looked up with OpenStreetMap (one lookup a second, cached), which can add a few seconds; lat and lon or a grid square need none. Cloud forecasts are cached for 10 minutes per area. A heavy call: one at a time per caller; another waits up to 20 seconds, then is refused as busy.

bands.description: radio scan only: keep satellites with a downlink in these bands: hf (3-30 MHz), wx (137 MHz weather), 2m (144-148 MHz), 70cm (420-450 MHz), l (1-2 GHz), s (2-4 GHz), other. Default: any band.

chart.description: true to also render the winning pass's polar sky chart (PNG, 800 by 897 pixels, about 120 KB) and return it in this same result. Default false.

lat.description: observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive (-90 to 90). Give it with lon, or give location instead.

limit.description: how many ranked passes to return, 1 to 20. Default 3.

location.description: where the observer is, when lat and lon are not given (they win when both are): a Maidenhead grid square (EN52, EN52ve, EN52ve12), coordinates in any common form ("41.88, -87.63", "41.88N 87.63W", "41°52'48"N 87°37'48"W", a Google Maps link or geo: URI), read locally, or a place name (city, address, landmark) looked up with OpenStreetMap.

lon.description: observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive and west negative (-180 to 180).

minElevation.description: lowest elevation that counts: a pass must climb above it, and rise and set are when it crosses it, in degrees above the horizon (0 to 90). Default 10.

mode.description: "visual" (default): naked-eye passes, sunlit while the sky is dark; "radio": every line-of-sight pass, day or night.

modes.description: radio scan only: keep satellites with a downlink of one of these kinds, matched on its mode or label, e.g. ["fm", "apt", "sstv"]. Default: any.

satellite.description: NORAD catalog number (as a number or a string) or a name, e.g. 25544, "25544" or "iss". Omit to scan: visual mode scans the popular satellites plus CelesTrak's visual group, radio mode every satellite with known downlinks.

skyType.description: how dark the observer's sky is, for the visual rating as on seeksat.com: "city" (stars to magnitude 3.5), "suburban" (stars to magnitude 4.5), "rural" (stars to magnitude 5.5), "dark" (stars to magnitude 6.5). Default "suburban".

windowHours.description: how far ahead to look, in hours, up to 240 (10 days). Default 72. With no satellite named, a visual scan stops at 168, and a radio scan defaults to 24 and stops at 72.
